reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: Characterised by recurrent, usually unilateral attacks of markedly raised intraocular pressure accompanied by mild, low-grade anterior uveitis
The striking feature is a large pressure rise that is disproportionate to the minimal inflammation present
Symptoms are often mild for the pressure level, with slight blurring, haloes, and mild discomfort rather than the severe pain of acute angle closure
Signs include a few fine keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium, faint aqueous cells, an open angle on gonioscopy, and often a corneal epithelial haze
Attacks are self-limiting over days to weeks and pressure returns to normal between episodes, but the same eye tends to be repeatedly affected
An association with cytomegalovirus in the aqueous has been recognised in some cases, and herpetic mechanisms are implicated
Treatment during an attack lowers pressure with topical agents and controls the inflammation with topical corticosteroids, while antiviral therapy is considered where a viral cause is suspected
Although classically benign, recurrent or prolonged attacks can lead to glaucomatous optic-nerve damage over time, so long-term monitoring is warranted
reference.pathophysiology: Posner-Schlossman syndrome produces episodic acute rises in intraocular pressure with concurrent mild anterior chamber inflammation affecting the trabecular outflow. During an attack, low-grade trabeculitis and inflammatory obstruction of an open angle reduce aqueous outflow while aqueous production may also be altered, producing a pressure spike out of proportion to the modest cellular reaction. The angle remains open, distinguishing it from angle-closure mechanisms. Infective triggers, particularly cytomegalovirus and other herpesviruses detected in the aqueous of some patients, are thought to drive the recurrent inflammation in a subset. Between crises the eye typically returns to normal, but repeated or protracted episodes can cumulatively damage the trabecular meshwork and optic nerve.
additionalDifferentials: Herpetic (herpes simplex or zoster) anterior uveitis with raised pressure
Primary open-angle glaucoma with an incidental mild uveitis
additionalInvestigations: Applanation tonometry during and between attacks to document the episodic pressure pattern
Gonioscopy to confirm an open angle and exclude angle closure
Slit-lamp examination for keratic precipitates and grading of anterior chamber activity
OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer and automated perimetry to detect cumulative glaucomatous damage
Aqueous sampling for cytomegalovirus or herpesvirus in recurrent or atypical cases
Baseline optic disc assessment for long-term comparison
redFlags: Very high pressure during an attack that could threaten the optic nerve if prolonged
Increasingly frequent, severe, or bilateral episodes suggesting a viral or alternative diagnosis
Emerging glaucomatous disc or field change indicating cumulative damage
Features atypical for the syndrome that raise concern for herpetic uveitis or angle closure
reference.prognosis: The visual prognosis is generally good because attacks are self-limiting and pressure normalises between episodes, but a minority develop chronic glaucomatous optic-nerve damage from recurrent crises, so periodic assessment of the disc and fields is advisable.
pitfalls: Mistaking the syndrome for acute angle-closure glaucoma because of the high pressure and haloes
Overtreating with prolonged corticosteroids and inducing a steroid pressure response
Assuming the condition is always benign and omitting long-term glaucoma surveillance
Missing an underlying cytomegalovirus or herpetic cause in recurrent cases
Failing to examine the angle and confirm it is open
management: Prompt intraocular-pressure reduction during attacks with topical aqueous-suppressants such as beta-blockers, alpha-agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, adding oral acetazolamide for marked pressure spikes
Short course of topical corticosteroid to settle the low-grade anterior chamber inflammation
Antiviral therapy with ganciclovir or aciclovir where cytomegalovirus or another herpesvirus is implicated in recurrent or atypical cases
Long-term surveillance of the optic disc, retinal nerve fibre layer and visual fields for cumulative glaucomatous damage from repeated crises
Glaucoma-lowering surgery for eyes developing chronic pressure elevation or optic-nerve damage refractory to medical control
Ongoing ophthalmology follow-up given the tendency for the same eye to be repeatedly affected
